q.intro.text: A line passes through the point A, negative two, seven, and the point B, four, negative two. What is its slope? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps, one line, three ways to write it. Press each step: the graph moves first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: Go from A to B. The run is four minus negative two, which is six. The rise is negative two minus seven, which is negative nine. B minus A on top and on the bottom: the slope is negative nine over six, which is negative three halves.

e.step1.text: Now take any point P, x, y, on the line. From A to P the slope is negative three halves too: a line has one slope everywhere. Multiply both sides by x plus two, and you get y minus seven equals negative three halves times x plus two. That is point-slope form: a point and the slope, in one equation.

e.step2.text: Get y alone. Negative three halves multiplies both terms in the bracket: y minus seven equals negative three halves x, minus three. Add seven: y equals negative three halves x, plus four. That is slope-intercept form, and the four is the y-intercept: the line crosses at zero, four.

e.step3.text: For standard form, clear the fraction: multiply by two, then put x and y on one side. Three x plus two y equals eight. Set y to zero and you get the zero, x equals eight thirds. Check B: three times four, plus two times negative two, is eight. It checks.

e.why.text: Quick check: why could any point P of the line go into the slope formula with A?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. That one fact gives point-slope form: the slope from a known point to every other point of the line is m.

e.why.first.text: Try it with B: y plus two equals negative three halves times x minus four. Get y alone, and it is y equals negative three halves x plus four again. Any point of the line works, and the equations look different but name one line.

e.why.slots.text: x and y stay letters: they stand for every point of the line. The numbers of A go in the slots x one and y one.

t.intro.text: Your turn: the line through C, negative one, five, and D, three, negative three. The slope is done for you: run four, rise negative eight, so the slope is negative two.

t.ps.text: Write the line in point-slope form, using C.

t.ps.ok.text: Yes: y minus five equals negative two times x plus one. The numbers of C go in with flipped signs, because point-slope form subtracts them.

t.ps.sign.text: Point-slope form subtracts the point: y minus five, and x minus negative one, which is x plus one. Your signs are flipped the other way.

t.ps.mix.text: That mixes the y of C with the x of D. Keep one point together: C is negative one, five.

t.b.text: Now get y alone: y equals negative two x plus b. What is b?

t.b.ok.text: Yes: y minus five equals negative two x minus two, so y equals negative two x plus three. The line crosses the y-axis at zero, three.

t.b.first.text: Five is the output of C, at x equals negative one, not at zero. Distribute the negative two, then add five.

t.b.part.text: Negative two multiplies both terms in the bracket: negative two times one is negative two, not one.

t.b.sign.text: Moving the minus five across the equals sign makes it plus five: y equals negative two x, minus two, plus five.

t.b.no.text: Distribute negative two to x and to one, then add five to both sides.

t.std.text: Last one: which is the standard form, A x plus B y equals C?

t.std.ok.text: Yes: two x plus y equals three. Set y to zero, and the zero is x equals three halves. Check D: two times three, plus negative three, is three. It checks.

t.std.sign.text: Moving negative two x across the equals sign makes it plus two x.

t.std.alone.text: That is slope-intercept form. Standard form has x and y together on one side.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked negative three halves, and you were right. Now you know why the order matters: B minus A, top and bottom.

q.cb.inv.text: At the start you picked negative two thirds. That puts the run on top. Slope is rise over run: the change in y first.

q.cb.order.text: At the start you picked three halves. That subtracts in opposite orders on top and bottom, which flips the sign. The line falls, so its slope is negative.

q.cb.none.text: Slope: the same order on top and bottom. Then one point and the slope give every form of the line.

p.intro.text: Riley finds the slope of the line through P, two, five, and Q, two, negative one: negative one minus five, divided by two minus two, is zero. Slope zero, so it is a flat line, and a function. Is Riley right?

p.test.text: Let’s test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: Right. The run is zero, and no number times zero gives negative six: the slope is undefined, not zero.

p.c2.text: Right. A flat line has a rise of zero over a real run: zero divided by four is zero. The points of Riley do not lie on a flat line.

p.c3.text: Right. Every point has x equal to two: the line is x equals two, a vertical line. One input with two outputs: not a function.

p.no.k0.text: Six divided by zero is not zero. If it were, zero times zero would be six. Dividing by zero has no answer.

p.no.none.text: No slope mixes up two different things. Slope zero is a flat line, and an undefined slope is a vertical line.

p.no.const.text: A rule like y equals five is a function: every input gets the one output five. That is not the problem here.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.done.text: That’s a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the graph backs every one. Zero slope is flat and a function. Undefined slope is vertical, and not a function.
